transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-12
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Martinez (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Quantaco ML Eng), Maya Chen (Quantaco PM), David Park (Quantaco Infra)

Summary (auto): cost/unit econ review, showed caching/batching numbers, agreed to larger benchmark and pricing follow-up

[00:00] Alex (AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, uh quick roll call?
[00:05] Jordan: Jordan here, morning
[00:06] Maya: Maya here
[00:07] David: David, good morning
[00:09] Priya (SE): Priya from Redwood, hi all
[00:12] Alex: cool, agenda is cost per token, tokens per second per dollar, caching savings we saw in last run, and batching tradeoffs — plan is to decide if we do a dedicated pilot next week

[02:10] Priya: quick note on the baseline run — we did three 100k token runs on the hosted endpoint with current quant profile (q4_8bit-ish) and avg throughput was about 1,200 tokens/sec on a p4-ish equivalent; cost approx $0.015 per 1k tokens which maps to roughly 0.08 tokens/sec per dollar across peak of the run, combining compute and I/O. the important part — when we enabled prefix/KV cache we saw a ~30-38% drop in token generation compute time depending on cache hit rate

[04:05] Jordan: sorry, can you repeat the tokens/sec per dollar number? I think I missed the unit there
[04:09] Priya: yeah so raw tokens/sec was 1,200, cost normalized to $ resulted in about 0.08 tokens per second per dollar in the baseline hosted run, with cache that moves to about 0.12 tokens/sec/$ so that's where the 35% improvement comes from

[06:00] Maya: that seems significant for us because about 60% of our queries are prefix-heavy — reused prompts for summarization. do you have hit rate distribution?
[06:08] Priya: we used the sample traffic you shared — hit rate was 52% cold start, warmed to about 67% within the run; that variability is why we recommended running a longer 1M token benchmark

[08:20] David: important for infra — can you confirm cache mode? was that per-shard KV cache or global prefix caching?
[08:28] Priya: it's KV cache at the runtime layer with prefix caching enabled for repeated prompts, it's not a global redis layer, it's internal to the serving runtime (we call it KV/prefix mix), sometimes the transcript shows it as K-V cache, or KV cache, a bit messy on the auto notes

[10:00] Alex: quick interjection — on batching vs latency, there's a hard tradeoff: larger batches get better tokens/sec/$ because GPU amortization improves, but 95th pct latency jumps. Quantaco's SLA is 300ms for interactive endpoints, right?
[10:12] Jordan: yes, 300ms for UI interactions — for background jobs we can push a lot higher

[11:05] Priya: we tested three batching profiles: conservative (max batch 8, target 50ms queue), medium (batch 32, 100ms queue), aggressive (batch 128, 250ms queue). conservative kept p95 under 280ms but throughput was lowest. The medium was a good compromise: p95 ~340ms occasionally spiking, tokens/sec/$ improved ~1.6x vs conservative. aggressive gave 2.8x tokens/sec/$ but p95 was typically >700ms which violates your interactive SLO

[13:00] Maya: could we do adaptive batching — small for UI endpoints and larger for background?
[13:06] Priya: absolutely — route by policy. Redwood runtime supports per-route batching and automatic fallback to lower-latency profiles when the request flag is set. Also you can pin model variants for latency sensitive routes

[14:30] Jordan: curious about dedicated vs hosted cost. based on your numbers what would dedicated look like for our expected qps of 40 rps with average 800 tokens per request?
[14:40] Alex: rough calc — at 40 rps * 800 tokens = 32k tokens/sec. With batching/quant and dedicated reserved GPU profile we estimate about 0.3 tokens/sec/$ effective after amortization (this is a simplified number), so you get better unit economics but incur fixed reserved cost. we provided a sample spreadsheet but will update it for your traffic shape

[16:45] David: can you send the math, I'm particularly worried about cost for peak 95th and tail latency when we scale up — do you model burst capacity?
[16:54] Alex: yes — dedicated comes with autoscale/burst pool options; we show two lanes: reserved steady-state plus burst on-demand. bursts increase unit cost for the bursted tokens but maintain SLOs. we'll add a scenario with 20% burst capacity and show blended unit cost

[18:30] Priya: one more thing on quantization: we benchmarked a q4 variant vs q8-like. q4 saved ~22% compute cost but sometimes increased failure-to-satisfy for specific prompts — quality regression for long-context summarization. quantization profile selection should be workload-driven

[20:00] Jordan: about the quality regressions — did you tie quality checks to evals? we have a set of policy prompts we run internally
[20:07] Priya: yes we run the eval suite; for q4 we saw a small drop in ROUGE on one of your summarization configs; we can run the evals on the 1M token run to get statistically significant numbers before recommending q4 for prod

[22:00] Maya: what's the expected savings if we combine good cache (70% hit) + medium batching + q6 profile? ballpark percent savings compared to hosted baseline
[22:10] Priya: ballpark: cache 35% improvement, medium batching 60% improvement, q6 another 15% from compute reduction — combined (multiplicative) roughly 2x cost reduction vs baseline hosted run; we'll put exact math in the spreadsheet because nominal additive/multiplicative depends on how much compute dominates cost vs egress/storage

[24:30] Jordan: any gotchas with the KV cache on private deployments? David is worried about eviction and memory footprint on small clusters
[24:38] Priya: on private/dedicated we allow config of cache size per node, eviction policy (LRU by default) and a persistent warm-up mechanism. eviction pressure shows up as more cold starts, which reduces hit rate. for small clusters we recommend a warmed prefix cache pre-seeded during deploys

[26:20] David: what's the operational overhead to run the dedicated pilot? any managed parts or full ops for us?
[26:29] Alex: Redwood Dedicated includes managed control plane with the option to have us manage the GPU pool; for private/on-prem you can opt for customer-managed nodes with our control plane; pilot can be fully managed for the first 4 weeks while you validate

[28:00] Maya: ok let's talk next steps — to be useful for the execs we'd need concrete cost-per-1M tokens and a canary plan
[28:08] Alex: confirmed — Priya will run 1M token benchmark with cache on/off + two batching profiles and q6/q4 variants; results CSV and plots. I'll update the cost model with reserved vs burst scenarios and a per-route cost table. David will give us sample traffic S3 and SLA doc so numbers align with real distribution

[30:10] Jordan: timeline? can we have results by next Tuesday?
[30:14] Priya: yes I can do the 1M run over the next 48 hours and have raw output by Monday EOD, polished by Tuesday

[32:00] Alex: we'll also include a short note on expected token/sec/$ for interactive vs batch jobs so you can present to finance

[33:10] Maya: a slightly separate ask — can you include security/compliance note for dedicated pilot? SOC2 audit status, encryption at rest, KMS?
[33:18] Alex: yes, I'll attach our security one-pager and SOC2 cert link. dedicated supports KMS-managed keys in private mode and HSM integrations; we'll include the details

[34:50] David: on competitors — we tried a quick run on vendor X (auto notes say 'open ay ai' sometimes) and their batching performed worse for long context; just flagging this for the bench deck

[36:00] Priya: noted, but we should be careful to compare apples to apples (same model variant, quant, and sequence lengths). we'll do head-to-head once you confirm the baseline model variant you want

[37:20] Jordan: sounds good. anything else?
[37:25] Alex: nope, quick recap of action items and owners then close
